title: Ecclesiastes 2:1–11
context: The Preacher turns from wisdom to pleasure as a test. He tries mirth, laughter, and wine, while keeping his heart guided by wisdom, to see what is good for people to do in their few days. He then describes vast projects: houses, vineyards, gardens and parks, pools, servants, herds, silver and gold, singers, and every delight, surpassing all before him in Jerusalem. The picture recalls the accounts of Solomon’s wisdom and wealth in 1 Kings 3–4 and 10, though the book does not name him. Yet when he surveys all his work, he finds it vanity and a chasing after wind, with no profit under the sun.

verses.text: I said in my heart, “Come now, I will test you with mirth; therefore enjoy pleasure;” and behold, this also was vanity.
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher decides to test his heart with mirth and pleasure, and finds that this too is vanity. Arminian readers note that the experiment is deliberate, an inquiry into whether pleasure can give lasting meaning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as beginning a test that will show pleasure cannot satisfy on its own terms. Both traditions read the experiment as instructive, not as a model for pursuing pleasure for its own sake.

verses.text: I said of laughter, “It is foolishness;” and of mirth, “What does it accomplish?”
verses.arminianNotes: He calls laughter foolishness and asks what mirth accomplishes. Arminian readers note that the Preacher does not condemn joy as such, but questions whether it can bear the weight of ultimate meaning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verdict as exposing the emptiness of pleasure sought as an end in itself. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse alongside 2:24–26, where enjoyment received from God is commended.

verses.text: I searched in my heart how to cheer my flesh with wine, my heart yet guiding me with wisdom, and how to lay hold of folly, until I might see what it was good for the sons of men that they should do under heaven all the days of their lives.
verses.arminianNotes: He tests how wine may cheer the flesh while wisdom still guides him, to see what is good for people to do. Arminian readers note the careful framing: the search is controlled by wisdom, not abandonment to excess.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the experiment as a sober inquiry into what is good in a short life. Both traditions read the verse as part of the Preacher’s test, and neither treats it as encouraging drunkenness.

verses.text: I made myself great works. I built myself houses. I planted myself vineyards.
verses.arminianNotes: He made great works, built houses, and planted vineyards. Arminian readers note the turn from pleasure to achievement, as the Preacher tests whether building and creating can give lasting satisfaction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as recalling the building works associated with Solomon in 1 Kings, though the book does not name him. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of a portrait of royal accomplishment.

verses.text: I made myself gardens and parks, and I planted trees in them of all kinds of fruit.
verses.arminianNotes: He made gardens and parks, planting fruit trees of all kinds. Arminian readers note the beauty and abundance of the projects, which some readers hear as echoing the garden imagery of Genesis 2.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers caution that any echo of Eden is a reading and not stated in the text. Both traditions read the verse as part of the Preacher’s catalog of great works undertaken in his search for meaning.

verses.text: I made myself pools of water, to water the forest where trees were grown.
verses.arminianNotes: He made pools of water to irrigate the forest of growing trees. Arminian readers note the practical engineering involved, showing the scale of resources at the Preacher’s command.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that irrigation on this scale required planning, labor, and wealth few could command. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse simply as part of the catalog, without drawing symbolic lessons from the pools.

verses.text: I bought male servants and female servants, and had servants born in my house. I also had great possessions of herds and flocks, above all who were before me in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: He acquired servants and great herds and flocks, more than all before him in Jerusalem. Arminian readers note that the list reflects the social world of ancient royalty, reported without endorsement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the accumulation as part of the Preacher’s test of whether possessions can satisfy. Both traditions read the verse as historical and literary portrait, not as a model for owning people.

verses.text: I also gathered silver and gold for myself, and the treasure of kings and of the provinces. I got myself male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men: musical instruments of all sorts.
verses.arminianNotes: He gathered silver, gold, royal treasure, singers, and every delight. Arminian readers note the echo of 1 Kings 10, where Solomon’s wealth is described, as a plain cross-reference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear in treasure, singers, and instruments the summit of what royal wealth could buy. Shared ground: this verse rounds off the catalog of riches, and both traditions take it as the setup for the verdict in 2:11.

verses.text: So I was great, and increased more than all who were before me in Jerusalem. My wisdom also remained with me.
verses.arminianNotes: He became great, surpassing all before him in Jerusalem, and his wisdom remained with him. Arminian readers note that he claims to have kept his judgment throughout, so the test was not clouded by folly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as stressing that the Preacher had every advantage. Both traditions read the note that his wisdom remained as important for the conclusion that follows in 2:11.

verses.text: Whatever my eyes desired, I didn’t keep from them. I didn’t withhold my heart from any joy, for my heart rejoiced because of all my labor, and this was my portion from all my labor.
verses.arminianNotes: He withheld nothing his eyes desired, and his heart rejoiced in his labor as his portion. Arminian readers note that the Preacher does find some joy in his work, a real portion even if it is not lasting.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the word “portion” as anticipating the book’s later teaching on enjoyment as God’s gift. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as acknowledging genuine pleasure within the limits of life under the sun.

verses.text: Then I looked at all the works that my hands had worked, and at the labor that I had labored to do; and behold, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no profit under the sun.
verses.arminianNotes: Surveying all his works, he finds them vanity and a chasing after wind, with no profit under the sun. Arminian readers see the honest conclusion that achievement and wealth cannot give final meaning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verdict as the climax of the experiment begun in 2:1. Both traditions read the verse as answering the question of 1:3, while the book continues to search for what is good.
